    **Left Column:**
    In the aquatic compartment, annual transports are of the same order of magnitude as contents. Most transport is thought to be by waterborne sediment.

Atmospheric pollution causes local, temporary changes within the atmospheric compartment that are very large in comparison with natural amounts. Industrial atmospheric emissions are variously estimated at 1035 to >360 Mg (150-400 tons) per year (Carson and Smith, 1975; Environmental Protection Agency, 1973), at concentrations ranging from ~10^-9 in city air to an extreme of 6 x 10^-6 measured in the smog water within the downwind plume from a copper smelter (J. Fletcher, 1976, personal communication). The other main source of silver pollution affecting the soil and surface waters is fertilizer, either Florida phosphates or processed sewage sludge (Carson and Smith, 1975). Qualities and concentrations so produced are currently unknown.

    Cloud seeding, if it became widespread, would result in local, temporary concentrations in precipitation of the same order of magnitude as the natural concentration in surface waters. Widespread and prolonged precipitation management, using silver iodide as the cloud-seeding agent and assuming that all the silver dispersed in the course of a century accumulated in the top 2 cm of soil, would not cause the silver concentration there to exceed the normal background.   - [Image #0] The image is a page from an academic paper titled "V. Generation and Application of Seeding Agents" and contains a discussion on the generation of seeding agents, specifically silver iodide (AgI), and its application in cloud seeding.
    
    The text on this page has been transcribed as follows:
    
    "1000°C, the AgI obviously sublimes from solid to vapor or evaporates from the molten state without ever actually boiling.
    
    Generators have been built in an amazing variety of ways. Although electric arcs are sometimes used, the AgI is usually vaporized in a flame, which may be continuous or associated with an explosion. Care is required to avoid prolonged exposure to a reducing atmosphere, which can decompose AgI to metallic silver and iodine vapor (I_(2)), with the latter often reacting with partially burned fuel to produce hydrogen iodide (HI).
    
    The two most common types of generators are the acetone generators and the pyrotechnic generators. A quite complete discussion of both types has been given by P. St.-Amand and his associates (Burkardt et al., 1970; St.-Amand et al., 1970a–c, 1971a–e; Vetter et al., 1970).
    
    The acetone generator originated with Vonnegut (1950). Because AgI is insoluble in acetone, a "carrier" or solubilizing agent is added. The most commonly used carriers are sodium iodide (NaI), potassium iodide (KI), and ammonium iodide (NH_(4)I). The acetone solution is sprayed into a flame and burned, either alone or with propane or gasoline, to vaporize the AgI and the carrier (Fig. 5.1). Silver iodide consumption rates have varied from as little as 5 g hr^(−1) up to almost 1 kg/hr^(−1).
    
    In some acetone generator configurations the heat is insufficient to vaporize the AgI completely. The product in such a-case includes sintered AgI, or a mixture containing AgI, with each particle representing the residue of one solution droplet. St.-Amand et al. (1971b, p. 33) considered this mode of operation acceptable for producing particles active as ice nuclei at temperatures close to 0°C. However, this mode is inefficient in terms of particle production, unless unrealistically fine sprays are assumed, and will not be discussed further.
    
    Liquid-fueled generators have been developed that use fuels in which AgI dissolves readily (Davis and Steele, 1968). These

    "Disappearing polymorph
    
    In materials science, a disappearing polymorph is a form of a crystal structure that is suddenly unable to be produced, instead transforming into a different crystal structure with the same chemical composition (a polymorph) during nucleation.[2][3] Sometimes the resulting transformation is extremely hard or impractical to reverse, because the new polymorph may be more stable.[4] It is hypothesized that contact with a single microscopic seed crystal of the new polymorph can be enough to start a chain reaction causing the transformation of a much larger mass of material.[5] Widespread contamination with such microscopic seed crystals may lead to the impression that the original polymorph has 'disappeared.'"

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand centers on the metaphor of 'crystallization' as a boundary object for understanding knowledge formation, technological lock-in, and consciousness itself. The arc begins with obscure scientific curiosities (disappearing polymorphs, Ice-9 references) and evolves into a multi-year discourse exploring how ideas, software defaults, and even cognitive structures can 'crystallize' into stable-but-arbitrary forms. The discussion is primarily constructive rather than dialectical—participants are riffing on the same metaphor across different domains (chemistry, software, culture, neuroscience) rather than challenging each other. While intellectually rich, it lacks a clear catalyst moment or real-world execution that would elevate it to an epic arc.

First explicit use of crystal formation as a learning metaphor (2020): 'growing crystals needs supersaturated solution'
Spiritual/philosophical expansion (2021): crystals as metaphor for order emerging from chaos, with persistent seeds
The viral catalyst (2024): Eshear's tweet about disappearing polymorphs reaches 3373 likes, making the concept mainstream
Eigenrobot's amplification connects disappearing polymorphs to false vacuum decay, expanding the metaphor's scope
Aleksil's synthesis: 'preconquest consciousness breaks down on contact with modernity' - applying crystallization to cultural evolution
DefenderOfBasic discovers SAE features form 'crystals' in concept space, bridging metaphor to AI interpretability
Lux extends the metaphor temporally: 'how crystals change over time, how they come to be, where they go'
Software defaults as crystallization: 'people work around standards until someone does something different and it spreads'
Ultimape's cloud seeding investigation: a parallel thread showing how scientific narratives themselves can crystallize around wrong framings
